literal: Taixing's younger brother Yao, styled Taiyuan.
idiomatic: Taixing's younger brother Yao, courtesy name Taiyuan.

literal: He had ability and standing; as Left Guard General he followed Gaozu on the southern campaign and was granted the rank Baron of Raoyang.
idiomatic: Talented and respected, he followed Gaozu south as Left Guard General and was made Baron of Raoyang.

literal: At the beginning of Shizong's reign he suffered his birth mother's death and memorialized asking to leave office; an edict said the residual-honor rule forbade it and did not allow.
idiomatic: Early in Shizong's reign he mourned his birth mother and asked to resign; an edict cited residual honor and refused.

literal: At the beginning of Suzong's reign he rose by stages to Left Grand Master of the Palace and still headed the Guard Army.
idiomatic: At Suzong's accession he rose to Left Grand Master of the Palace while still commanding the Guard Army.

literal: He was transferred to inspector of Jizhou.
idiomatic: He was made inspector of Jizhou.

literal: [4]Yao, because the various Hu previously had no household registers and good and bad could not be distinguished, ordered them all to compile registers.
idiomatic: [4]Because the frontier Hu had no household registers and criminals could not be told from honest men, Yao ordered every household registered.

literal: He also had the various Hu registered;
idiomatic: He also registered the Hu clans;

literal: he meant to tax them to fill military needs.
idiomatic: he meant to tax them to fund the army.

literal: The Hu were unwilling and together framed Yao, saying he took bribes of gold and horses.
idiomatic: The Hu resisted and jointly accused Yao of taking gold and horses in bribes.

literal: The censorate investigated; the facts agreed with the Hu's charge, and Yao was dismissed and struck from the rolls.
idiomatic: The censorate investigated, found the charges matched, and Yao was removed and struck from office.

literal: Yao pleaded his innocence without cease; an edict ordered the offices to reinvestigate, and he was cleared.
idiomatic: Yao protested his innocence until an edict ordered a new inquiry and he was cleared.

literal: He was made Right Grand Master of the Palace.
idiomatic: He was restored as Right Grand Master of the Palace.

literal: At that time in Jizhou the monk Fazheng had turned to heterodox sorcery and persuaded the Bohai man Li Guibo; Guibo's whole household followed him, he gathered fellow villagers, and they made Fazheng their leader.
idiomatic: In Jizhou the monk Fazheng had taken up demonic sorcery and won over Li Guibo of Bohai; Guibo's household and neighbors followed, and they set Fazheng at their head.

literal: Fazheng made Guibo Ten-Abiding Bodhisattva, Pacifying-Demons Army Marshal, and King Who Settles Han; he styled himself "Mahayana."
idiomatic: Fazheng named Guibo Ten-Abiding Bodhisattva, Marshal of the Army That Pacifies Demons, and King Who Settles the Han, while he called himself Mahayana.

literal: Whoever killed one man was a One-Abiding Bodhisattva; whoever killed ten was a Ten-Abiding Bodhisattva.
idiomatic: One murder made a One-Abiding Bodhisattva; ten murders made a Ten-Abiding Bodhisattva.

literal: They also mixed mad drugs; whoever took them no longer knew father, brother, or son, and knew only killing.
idiomatic: They brewed frenzy-drugs; under their spell kin no longer recognized one another and knew only slaughter.

literal: Thereupon they gathered a mob, killed the magistrate of Fucheng, stormed Bohai commandery, and slaughtered officials and clerks.
idiomatic: They raised a mob, killed Fucheng's magistrate, stormed Bohai commandery, and butchered officials and clerks.

literal: Inspector Xiao Baoyin sent Acting Chief Clerk Cui Bolin to attack them; he was defeated at Zhuzao city and died in battle.
idiomatic: Inspector Xiao Baoyin sent Acting Chief Clerk Cui Bolin against them; Bolin was beaten at Zhuzao city and killed.

literal: The rebels then swelled; wherever they went they massacred monasteries, cut down monks and nuns, burned sutras and images, saying a new Buddha had come to clear away the old demons.
idiomatic: The rebels swelled, razing monasteries, slaughtering monks and nuns, and burning sutras and icons, proclaiming a new Buddha come to sweep away the old demons.

literal: An edict made Yao bearer of the staff, commander of all armies on the northern expedition, and he led a hundred thousand foot and horse to suppress them.
idiomatic: Yao was commissioned bearer of the staff, commander of the northern expedition, and led a hundred thousand foot and horse against them.

literal: Fazheng together attacked Yao; Yao defeated them all.
idiomatic: Fazheng massed to strike Yao; Yao broke every attack.

literal: Yao sent the Assistant General Who Supports the State Zhang Niu and others with cavalry in pursuit; they routed the band, captured Fazheng with his wife the nun Huihui and the rest, beheaded them, and sent the heads to the capital.
idiomatic: Yao sent Assistant General Zhang Niu and others in pursuit; they crushed the sect, seized Fazheng with his wife the nun Huihui, beheaded them, and sent the heads to the capital.

literal: Later Guibo was captured and executed at the capital market.
idiomatic: Guibo was later taken and executed in the capital market.

literal: At first Yao and his brothers in greater mourning were all grandsons of Gongzong; by Suzong's time the original mourning tie was exhausted, so Yao and the rest were struck from the imperial registry.
idiomatic: Yao and his brothers had worn greater mourning for Gongzong; by Suzong's reign that original tie was spent, and they were removed from the imperial registry.

literal: Yao memorialized: "I have heard that the sage faces south to hear all under Heaven; what cannot be altered are kinship and honor.
idiomatic: Yao memorialized: "I hear that the sage faces south to rule the realm; what cannot be changed are kinship and honor."

literal: At the fourth generation the finest mourning ends; at the fifth the bared shoulder; at the sixth, kinship is exhausted.
idiomatic: At the fourth generation the finest mourning ends; at the fifth the shoulder is bared; at the sixth, kinship is spent."

literal: Beyond that, men are still bound by surname without division, and joined by food without distinction.
idiomatic: Beyond that, men still share a surname without being severed, and share a meal without being set apart."

literal: The law also says that in deliberating kin, one counts not only the present generation's kin but the former emperor's five generations.
idiomatic: The law also says that in weighing kin one counts not only the living generation but the former emperor's five generations."

literal: Carefully tracing this intent, it is meant to broaden the imperial clan and weight the foundation stones.
idiomatic: Tracing that intent, it was meant to widen the imperial house and steady the realm's pillars."

literal: The reason the late emperor altered this statute and made this separate rule was that in the Taihe years he had his mind on Wu and Shu; the costs of beginning were feared at the start, and the cuts arose only for the moment.
idiomatic: The late emperor changed this statute only because in the Taihe years his mind was on Wu and Shu; startup costs frightened him at the outset, and the cuts were a temporary measure."

literal: Moreover Prince Ti of Huaiyang, at the very start of being struck from the registry, received three thousand bolts of silk from Gaozu to mark the weight of separation;
idiomatic: When Prince Ti of Huaiyang was first struck from the rolls, Gaozu gave him three thousand bolts of silk to mark how heavy the parting was;

literal: Prince Changming of Leliang also received two thousand bolts of silk to preserve affectionate regard.
idiomatic: Prince Changming of Leliang received two thousand bolts to preserve affectionate regard.

literal: These were all the former court's earnest, compelled thought—things done because there was no choice.
idiomatic: Those were all the former court's reluctant concessions—things done because there was no choice."

literal: The ancients said that even a centipede does not stiffen until death because those who aid it are many.
idiomatic: The ancients said a centipede does not stiffen until death because so many legs still support it."

literal: Your servant truly does not wish rashly to climb the great stairs or seek to fatten his house, but it wounds me that the great house loses a share and the Son of Heaven's registry holds barely a dozen names.
idiomatic: I do not seek to climb high or swell my household, but it grieves me that the great house loses a branch and the Son of Heaven's registry holds barely a dozen names."

literal: Under Han, kings' sons were not limited in number—all received fiefs as marquises; by Wei and Jin none failed to broaden enfeoffments across rivers and mountains and style them dukes, because they hated that the great house was not firm and the bone-and-flesh bond had grown thin.
idiomatic: Under Han every king's son, however many, received a fief as marquis; under Wei and Jin enfeoffments sprawled across the land as dukes, for they feared a weak great house and thinning kinship."

literal: Your servant, though five generations from the present sovereign, to the late emperor was still the Son of Heaven's grandson; Gaozu therefore restored state rank, salary, and grain, again granting food and clothing—while the empress's kin received grain but not clothing, wishing to separate inner from outer and mark the difference.
idiomatic: Though I stand five generations from Your Majesty, to the late emperor I was still the Son of Heaven's grandson; Gaozu restored rank, salary, and grain and again granted food and clothing—whereas the empress's kin received grain but not clothing, to mark inner from outer."

literal: Now the feeling owed the ancestral temples is not yet forgotten in the heart;
idiomatic: The debt owed the ancestral temples is not yet forgotten;

literal: the grief of walking the rites has suddenly already arrived.
idiomatic: the grief of walking the mourning rites has suddenly come upon us."

literal: For all who hold fiefs, on the day they die, when the three-year mourning ends, only then should titles be altered and taken away.
idiomatic: For every enfeoffed prince, only when three years' mourning after his death is finished should titles be altered or withdrawn."

literal: Now the court is still in the stifled-grief period, yet this matter is already debated—truly it is not yet fitting."
idiomatic: The court is still in stifled grief, yet this is already debated—truly the time is not right."

literal: An edict sent the memorial to the Masters of Writing for broad deliberation and report.
idiomatic: An edict referred the memorial to the Masters of Writing for broad deliberation.

literal: Minister of State Prince Cheng of Rencheng and Left Vice Minister Yuan Hui memorialized agreement with Yao's table.
idiomatic: Minister of State Prince Cheng of Rencheng and Left Vice Minister Yuan Hui memorialized in agreement with Yao.

literal: Empress Dowager Ling did not follow.
idiomatic: Empress Dowager Ling would not agree.

literal: He died; posthumous title Duke Xuan.
idiomatic: He died and was posthumously titled Duke Xuan.

literal: Yao's younger brother Heng, styled Jing'an, had rough knowledge of books and history.
idiomatic: Yao's brother Heng, courtesy name Jing'an, had a rough schooling in the classics and histories.

literal: Heng, following the Spring and Autumn principle that names do not take mountains and rivers, memorialized asking to change his name to Zhi.
idiomatic: Following the Spring and Autumn rule that names do not borrow mountains and rivers, Heng asked to change his name to Zhi.

literal: [5]By successive posts he was Director of the Imperial Sacrifices, Director of the Secretariat, and Palace Attendant.
idiomatic: [5]He rose to Director of the Imperial Sacrifices, Director of the Secretariat, and Palace Attendant.

literal: Later he was killed at Heyin.
idiomatic: He was later killed at Heyin.

literal: Posthumously given Grand Tutor and Duke of the State, posthumous title Duke Xuanmu.
idiomatic: He was posthumously made Grand Tutor and Duke of the State with the title Duke Xuanmu.

literal: Xiao Xincheng, Prince of Jiyin, was enfeoffed in the second year of Heping.
idiomatic: Xiao Xincheng, Prince of Jiyin, received his fief in Heping year 2.

literal: He had considerable military talent.
idiomatic: He showed real talent in war.

literal: When the Kumo Xi raided the borders, an edict ordered Xincheng to lead troops against them.
idiomatic: When the Kumo Xi raided the frontier, Xincheng was ordered to lead troops against them.

literal: Xincheng made much poisoned wine; as the bandits pressed in he abandoned camp and left.
idiomatic: Xincheng brewed great stores of poisoned wine; as the enemy closed in he abandoned camp and withdrew.

literal: When the bandits arrived they rejoiced and competed to drink, and for a time were wholly unprepared.
idiomatic: The raiders came, drank eagerly, and for a while had no guard up.

literal: He then chose light horse, and while they were drunk struck freely, taking many captives and heads.
idiomatic: He then led light cavalry and struck the drunk camp, taking many prisoners and heads.

literal: Later he was Director of the Outer Palace.
idiomatic: He later became Director of the Outer Palace.

literal: He died; posthumously made Grand General, posthumous title Duke Hui.
idiomatic: He died and was posthumously made Grand General with the title Duke Hui.

literal: His son Yu, styled Fusheng, inherited.
idiomatic: His son Yu, courtesy name Fusheng, succeeded.

literal: He held the rank of Opening the Government.
idiomatic: He held the rank that opens the government.

literal: As inspector of Xuzhou, for corruption he was sentenced to death and the state was abolished.
idiomatic: As Xuzhou inspector he was executed for corruption and the fief abolished.

literal: His eldest son Bi, styled Yongming, was upright and had literary learning.
idiomatic: His eldest son Bi, courtesy name Yongming, was upright and literate.

literal: He held the post Central Scattered Grandee.
idiomatic: He served as Central Scattered Grandee.

literal: As the legitimate heir he should have inherited the former title, but his uncle Li, Vice Minister of the Masters of Writing, through the Yu clan's favor seized Bi's princely title and forcibly gave it to his uterine brother's son Dan.
idiomatic: As legitimate heir he should have taken the title, but his uncle Li, Vice Minister of the Masters of Writing, used the Yu family's favor to strip Bi and hand the fief to his uterine brother's son Dan.

literal: Thereupon Bi wholly abandoned worldly affairs, pleaded illness, and returned to his private house.
idiomatic: Bi then abandoned public life, pleaded illness, and withdrew to his house.

literal: Shizong summoned him as Palace Attendant; Bi memorialized firmly declining.
idiomatic: Shizong summoned him as Palace Attendant; Bi firmly declined by memorial.

literal: He entered Mount Song, made a cave his chamber, and wore plain cloth and ate vegetables.
idiomatic: He went to Mount Song, lived in a cave, and ate coarse greens in plain cloth.

literal: He died.
idiomatic: He died.

literal: In the first year of Jianyi, his son Huiye memorialized to restore the princely title.
idiomatic: In Jianyi year 1 his son Huiye petitioned to restore the princely title.

literal: In the third year of Yong'an he was posthumously made Director of the Masters of Writing, Duke of the State, posthumous title Wenxian.
idiomatic: In Yong'an year 3 he was posthumously made Director of the Masters of Writing and Duke of the State with the title Wenxian.

literal: At first Bi once dreamed a man told him: "Your person cannot pass on a worldly fief; he who continues the former title will be your eldest son Shaoyuan."
idiomatic: Bi once dreamed a voice saying, "You will not hold the fief in life; your eldest son Shaoyuan will restore the line."

literal: Bi awoke and at once told Huiye.
idiomatic: He woke and told Huiye at once.

literal: In the end it was as the words said.
idiomatic: In the end it came to pass as he had said.

literal: Huiye in youth was treacherous and shallow and often trafficked with bandits.
idiomatic: Huiye in youth was treacherous and shallow and trafficked with bandits.

literal: Growing older he changed his ways, studied the histories, also wrote somewhat, and was generous with resolute purpose.
idiomatic: He later reformed, read histories, wrote a little, and grew generous and resolute.

literal: By successive posts he was Duke of Works, Grand Marshal, with added special advancement, Director of the Secretariat, and Recorder of the Masters of Writing.
idiomatic: He rose to Duke of Works and Grand Marshal, with special advancement, Director of the Secretariat, and Recorder of the Masters of Writing.

literal: Prince Wenxiang of Qi once asked him: "What have you been reading lately?"
idiomatic: Prince Wenxiang of Qi once asked him, "What have you been reading lately?"

literal: He replied: "I often trace the stories of Yi and Huo; I do not read the books of Cao and Sima."
idiomatic: He answered, "I keep to the tales of Yi Yin and Huo Guang; I do not read the books of the Caos and Simas."

literal: Huiye, seeing the times gradually decline, no longer plotted to preserve himself whole but devoted himself only to eating and drinking—three sheep a day, a calf every three days.
idiomatic: Seeing the age fail, Huiye gave up saving himself whole and gave himself to feasting—three sheep a day, a calf every three days.

literal: He also once composed a poem: "Once the royal way was tranquil, and hosts of worthies flourished."
idiomatic: He once wrote: "Once the royal way was tranquil, and hosts of worthies flourished."

literal: Now we meet a blocked age, and foxes and hares throng unchecked."
idiomatic: "Now the road is blocked, and foxes and hares run wild."

literal: At the beginning of Qi he was demoted to Duke of Meiyang county, Opening the Government, Pillar of State, and special advancement.
idiomatic: At Qi's founding he was demoted to Duke of Meiyang county with the ranks Opening the Government, Pillar of State, and special advancement.

literal: When Huiye was at Jinyang he kept no social ties; in his usual leisure he compiled the genealogies of Wei princes and kings, titled Records for Distinguishing the Imperial Clan, forty juan, and it circulated in the world.
idiomatic: At Jinyang he kept to himself; in idle hours he compiled the genealogies of Wei princes into the Records for Distinguishing the Imperial Clan in forty juan, which circulated widely.

literal: Huiye's younger brother Zhaoye had considerable learning; he held the post Remonstrating Grandee.
idiomatic: Huiye's brother Zhaoye was learned and served as Remonstrating Grandee.

literal: When Emperor Zhuang was about to visit the southern capital, Zhaoye stood outside the Changhe Gate, seized the horse's bridle and remonstrated; the emperor avoided him and passed by, then later comforted and encouraged him.
idiomatic: When Emperor Zhuang meant to visit the southern capital, Zhaoye stood at the Changhe Gate, seized the bridle, and remonstrated; the emperor passed around him, then later praised him.

literal: He held the posts Attendant-in-Ordinary of the Yellow Gate, Guards General, and Right Grand Master of the Palace.
idiomatic: He served as Attendant-in-Ordinary of the Yellow Gate, Guards General, and Right Grand Master of the Palace.

literal: He died; posthumous title Marquis Wen.
idiomatic: He died and was posthumously titled Marquis Wen.

literal: Yu's younger brother Yan, styled Zhongxuan, held the post Grand Master of the Palace.
idiomatic: Yu's brother Yan, courtesy name Zhongxuan, was Grand Master of the Palace.

literal: He died.
idiomatic: He died.

literal: His son Fu, styled Boyi, inherited.
idiomatic: His son Fu, courtesy name Boyi, succeeded.

literal: At the beginning of Zhuang's reign he was made to petition through his cousin Huiye to recover the princely title.
idiomatic: Early in Zhuang's reign he petitioned through his cousin Huiye to recover the princely title.

literal: Made inspector of Yongzhou, his government was harsh and cruel, and officials and people suffered under it.
idiomatic: As Yongzhou inspector he ruled with harsh cruelty, and officials and people groaned under him.

literal: When his wife Lady Cui bore a son, Li at once released from the provincial prison those condemned to death and all exiles and convicts whose cases had not yet reached the central offices.
idiomatic: When his wife Lady Cui bore a son, Li emptied the provincial prison of the condemned and every exile whose case had not yet reached the capital.

literal: Transferred to inspector of Jizhou, he entered the capital as Left Vice Minister of the Masters of Writing.
idiomatic: Moved to Jizhou, he then entered the capital as Left Vice Minister of the Masters of Writing.

literal: The emperor asked: "I hear that in the province you killed without reason, wronged many, and also killed many monks in great numbers."
idiomatic: The emperor said, "I hear that in your province you killed without cause, wronged many, and slaughtered monks in great numbers."

literal: He replied: "Your servant in Jizhou could kill only about two hundred monks—how is that many?"
idiomatic: He answered, "In Jizhou I killed only some two hundred monks—how is that many?"

literal: The emperor said: "If one creature does not obtain its place, it is as though one were cast into a moat—how much more when two hundred monks are killed and you say it is not many."
idiomatic: The emperor said, "If a single creature is wronged it is as though cast into a ditch—how then when two hundred monks die and you call it few?"

literal: Li removed his cap and apologized; he was granted a seat.
idiomatic: Li doffed his cap and apologized; he was given a seat.

literal: He died; posthumous title Wei.
idiomatic: He died and was posthumously titled Wei.

literal: His son Xianhe in youth had integrity; he held the post Recorder of the Masters of Writing in the Department of State.
idiomatic: His son Xianhe in youth had integrity and served as Recorder in the Department of State.
